(4.56) Although the notation here appears bit tedious, the idea of PPO is simple: we develop an objective by combining the clipped likelihood ratio of the target and reference policies with an advantage function, and then impose penalty that ensures policy updates are not too large. The PPO-based RLHF is illustrated in Figure 4.9. To summarize, implementing RLHF requires building four models, all based on the Transformer decoder architecture. Reward Model (rϕ() where ϕ denotes the parameters). The reward model learns from human preference data to predict the reward for each pair of input and output token sequences. It is Transformer decoder followed by linear layer that maps sequence (the concatenation of the input and output) to real-valued reward score. Value Model or Value Function (Vω() where ω denotes the parameters). The value function receives reward scores from the reward model and is trained to predict the expected sum of rewards that can be obtained starting from state. It is generally based on the same architecture as the reward model. Reference Model (πθref () = Prθref () where θref denotes the parameters). The reference model is the baseline LLM that serves as starting point for policy training. In RLHF, it represents the previous version of the model or model trained without human feedback. It is used to sample output sequences and contribute to the loss computation for policy training. Target Model or Policy (πθ() = Prθ() where θ denotes the parameters). This policy governs how the LLM decides the most appropriate next token given its context. It is trained under the supervision of both the reward model and the value model. In practice, these models need to be trained in certain order. First, we need to initialize them using existing models. For example, the reward model and the value model can be initialized with pre-trained LLM, while the reference model and the target model can be initialized with model that has been instruction fine-tuned. Note that, at this point, the reference model is ready for use and will not be further updated. Second, we need to collect human preference data and train the reward model on this data. Third, both the value model and the policy are trained simultaneously using the reward model. sections.title: 4.4 Improved Human Preference Alignment
sections.content: In the previous section, we reviewed the basic concepts of reinforcement learning and the general framework of RLHF. In this section, we will discuss some refinements of RLHF and alternative methods to achieve human preference alignment.

sections.title: 4.4.1 Better Reward Modeling
sections.content: In Section 4.3.2, we highlighted the task of learning from human preferences as well as the use of pairwise ranking loss for training reward models. Here we consider more methods for reward modeling. Our discussion will be relatively general, and since the reward model is widely used in many reinforcement learning problems, it will be easy for us to apply the methods discussed here to RLHF and related applications.

sections.title: 4.4.1.1 Supervision Signals
sections.content: The training of reward models can broadly be seen as ranking problem, where the model learns to assign scores to outputs such that the resulting ranking reflects the preferences indicated by humans. There are several approaches to training reward models from ranking perspective. One approach is to extend pairwise ranking to listwise ranking. For each sample in dataset, we can use the LLM to generate multiple outputs, and ask human experts to order these outputs. For example, given set of four outputs {y1, y2, y3, y4}, one possible ordering of these outputs can be y2 y3 y1 y4. straightforward way to model such rankings is to sum the pairwise comparison losses. For example, we can define the listwise loss by accumulating the loss over all pairs of outputs: Llist = E(x,Y )Dr h

An extension to the Bradley-Terry model for listwise ranking could involve ranking mechanism that takes into account the entire list of outputs rather than just pairwise comparisons. One such model is the Plackett-Luce model, which generalizes the Bradley-Terry model to handle multiple items in ranking [Plackett, 1975]. In the Plackett-Luce model, for each item in list, we define worth for this item that reflects its relative strength of being chosen over other items. For the reward modeling problem here, the worth of in the list can be defined as α(y) = exp(r(x, y)). (4.61) There are also many other pairwise and listwise methods for modeling rankings, such as RankNet [Burges et al., 2005] and ListNet [Cao et al., 2007]. All these methods can be categorized into large family of learning-to-rank approaches, and most of them are applicable to the problem of modeling human preferences. However, discussing these methods is beyond the scope of this chapter. Interested readers may refer to books on this topic for more details [Liu, 2009; Li, 2011]. In addition to pairwise and listwise ranking, pointwise methods provide an alternative way to train reward models and capture human preferences. Unlike methods that focus on the relative rankings between different outputs, pointwise methods treat each output independently. For example, human experts might assign score to an individual output, such as rating on five-point scale. The objective is to adjust the reward model so that its outputs align with these scores. simple way to achieve pointwise training is through regression techniques where the reward of each output is treated as target variable. Let φ(x, y) be the score assigned to given by humans. Pointwise reward models can be trained by minimizing loss function, often based on mean squared error or other regression losses, between the predicted reward r(x, y) and the actual human feedback φ(x, y). For example, the loss function could be Lpoint = E(x,y)Dr (cid:2)(φ(x, y) r(x, y))2(cid:3). (4.62)

sections.title: While pointwise methods are conceptually simpler and can directly guide the reward model to
sections.content: 4.4 Improved Human Preference Alignment 189 predict scores, they might not always be the best choice in RLHF. problem is that these methods may struggle with high variance in human feedback, especially when different experts provide inconsistent scores for similar outputs. Because they focus on fitting to absolute scores rather than relative differences, inconsistencies in scoring can lead to poor model performance. Moreover, fitting to specific scored outputs might hurt generalization, particularly given that training data is often very limited in RLHF. In contrast, methods that consider relative preferences can promote the learning of more generalized preference patterns. Nevertheless, there are scenarios where pointwise methods might still be suitable. For example, in tasks where training data is abundant and the costs of obtaining accurate, consistent annotations are low, pointwise methods can prove effective. In fact, to make the supervision signal for training the reward model more robust, we can also introduce additional regularization terms into training. For example, if we consider the first term Uppo-clip(x, y; θ) in Eq. Another example is that Eisenstein et al. Optimizing with this regularization term can help mitigate the underdetermination of reward models5.

sections.title: 4.4.1.2 Sparse Rewards vs. Dense Rewards
sections.content: As discussed in Section 4.3, the rewards provided by human feedback are typically sparse: they are observed only at the end of sequences, rather than continuously throughout the generation process. Dealing with sparse rewards has long been concern in reinforcement learning, and has been one of the challenges in many practical applications. For example, in robotics, reward functions often need to be shaped to ease optimization rather than relying only on end-of-sequence rewards. Various methods have been developed to address this issue. One common approach is reward shaping, where the original function is modified to include intermediate rewards, thereby providing more immediate feedback. Also, one can adopt curriculum learning to sequence tasks such that their complexity gradually increases. This can help models master simpler tasks first and gradually prepare them for more complex challenges. There are many such methods that can mitigate the impact of sparse rewards, such as intrinsic motivation and hindsight experience replay. Most of these methods are general and discussed extensively in the broader reinforcement learning literature, such as the seminal textbook by Sutton and Barto [2018]. Although we do not discuss methods for mitigating sparse rewards in detail here, an interesting question arises: why are sparse rewards so successful in RLHF? Recall from Section 4.3.1 that the supervision signal received at each time step is not the reward for the current action, but 5A model is called underdetermined if there are multiple alternative sets of parameters that can achieve the same objective. 190 Alignment rather some form of the accumulated rewards from until the last time step. Such supervision signals are dense over the sequence, because the reward obtained at the end of the sequence can be transferred back to that time step, regardless of which time step it is. In other words, the sparse rewards are transformed into the dense supervision signals. Furthermore, from the perspective of reward shaping, Ng et al. [1999] show that the reward at is computed as r(st, at, st+1) = r(st, at, st+1) + (st, at, st+1), (4.64) where r() is the transformed reward function, r() is the original reward function, and () is the shaping reward function. To ensure the optimality of the policy under the transformed reward function, the shaping reward function can be given in the form (st, at, st+1) = γΦ(st+1) Φ(st), (4.65) where Φ(s) is called the potential value of the state s. If we define Φ(s) as the value function as in Eq. (4.15) and substitute Eq. (4.65) into Eq. (4.64), we obtain r(st, at, st+1) = r(st, at, st+1) + γV (st+1) (st). (4.66) It is interesting to see that this expression is equivalent to the one-step temporal-difference error used in PPO. This relates advantage-based methods to reward shaping: the advantage is essentially shaped reward. On the other hand, one of the reasons for adopting end-of-sequence rewards lies in the nature of the RLHF tasks. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning environments where the agent interacts with dynamic environment, RLHF tasks often involve complex decision-making based on linguistic or other high-level cognitive processes. These processes do not lend themselves easily to frequent and meaningful intermediate rewards because the quality and appropriateness of the actions can only be fully evaluated after observing their impact in the larger context of the entire sequence or task. In this case, the reward signals based on human feedback, though very sparse, are typically very informative and accurate. Consequently, this sparsity, together with the high informativeness and accuracy of the human feedback, can make the learning both robust and efficient.

sections.title: 4.4.1.3 Fine-grained Rewards
sections.content: For many applications, our objective will be more complex than merely evaluating an entire text. For example, in sentiment analysis, we often do not just determine the sentiment of text, but need to analyze the sentiment in more detail by associating it with specific aspects of topic discussed in the text. Consider the sentence The camera of the phone is excellent, but the battery life is disappointing. In this example, we would need to separately analyze the sentiments expressed about the camera and the battery. Such analysis, known as aspect-based sentiment analysis, helps provide finer-grained understanding of the customer review compared to general sentiment analysis. For the problem of reward modeling, we often need to model different parts of sequence at similarly fine-grained level. straightforward way to achieve this is to divide sequence into distinct segments and compute reward for each segment independently [Wu et al., 2023b]. 4.4 Improved Human Preference Alignment 191 Suppose an output token sequence can be divided into ns segments {y1, ..., yns} based on some criterion. We can then use the reward model to evaluate each of these segments. By taking the input x, the full output y, and the specific segment yk into account, the reward score for the k-th segment is given by rk = r(x, y, yk). (4.67) The total reward score for the entire output sequence is then simply the sum of these segment-level rewards r(x, y) = nsX k=1 r(x, y, yk). (4.68) This reward r(x, y) can then be used to train the policy via standard RL algorithms like PPO. problem with this approach is that training reward models at the segment level is not as straightforward as learning from human preferences on entire texts, as it is difficult to obtain segment-level human preference data. For rating-like problems (e.g., we rate segment according to its level of misinformation), one simple approach is to assign rating score to each segment and train the reward model using pointwise methods. For example, we can use strong LLM to rate the sequences y1...yk1 and y1...yk, and obtain the scores s(y1...yk1) and s(y1...yk). We can then define the score of the segment yk as the difference between s(y1...yk) and s(y1...yk1) s(yk) = s(y1...yk) s(y1...yk1). (4.69) Using these segment-level scores, we can train the reward model with regression loss function Lrating = E(x,y,yk)Dr (cid:2)(s(yk) r(x, y, yk))2(cid:3). (4.70) Sometimes, alignment can be treated as classification problem, for example, we assess whether segment has ethical issues. In this case, the segment can be labeled as ethical or unethical, either by humans or using additional classifiers. Given these discrete labels, we can train the reward model using classification loss functions. Suppose the ground truth label is ˆr {1, 1}, where 1 indicates an unethical segment and 1 indicates an ethical one, and let r(x, y, yk) represent the scalar output produced by the reward model6. The reward model can then be trained using the hinge loss: Lhinge = E(x,y,yk)Dr (cid:2) max(0, 1 r(x, y, yk) ˆr)(cid:3), (4.71) where ˆr {1, 1} denotes the ground truth label. The remaining issue here is how to split into segments. One approach is to define fixedlength segmentation, where is divided into equal-length chunks. However, this may not always be ideal, as the content of the sequence may not align well with fixed boundaries. An alternative 6To allow the reward model to output classification probabilities or logits, we can adapt the linear layer described in Section 4.3.2 accordingly. 192 Alignment approach is to segment based on specific linguistic or semantic cues, such as sentence boundaries, topic shifts, or other meaningful structures in the text. Such segmentation can be achieved by using linguistic segmentation systems or prompting LLMs to identify natural breaks in the sequence. Another approach is to use dynamic segmentation methods based on the complexity of the sequence. For example, segments could be defined where there is significant change in the reward score, which might correspond to shifts in the task being modeled. 4.4.1.4 Combination of Reward Models reward model can be viewed as proxy for the environment. Since the true environment is often too complex or unknown, developing perfect proxy for the environment is generally not possible. As result, over-aligning LLMs with this imperfect proxy might lead to decreased performance, known as the overoptimization problem [Stiennon et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023a]7. We can also explain this through Goodharts law, which states: when measure becomes target, it ceases to be good measure [Goodhart, 1984]. Addressing the overoptimization problem is not easy, and no fully satisfactory solution currently exists. The ideal approach might be to develop an oracle reward model that can perfectly capture the true objectives of the task and prevent the agent from tricking. However, creating such model is extremely difficult due to the complexity of the real-world environment, as well as the challenge of defining all the relevant factors that contribute to the desired outcome. Instead, more practical approach is to combine multiple reward models, thereby reducing the mismatch between the training objective and the true objective that arises from using single reward model [Coste et al., 2024]. Combining set of reward models is conceptually straightforward and can often be formulated as an ensemble learning problem. simple yet common approach is to combine the outputs of these models to obtain more reliable reward estimation: rcombine = k=1 wk rk(x, y), (4.72) where rk() is the k-th reward model in the ensemble, wk is the weight of rk(), and is the number of reward models. This combined reward can then be used to supervise the training of policy. In fact, there are many ways to combine different models, for example, one can make predictions using Bayesian model averaging or develop fusion network to learn to combine the predictions from different models. Alternatively, one can frame this task as multi-objective optimization problem, and use multiple reward models to train the policy simultaneously. These methods have been extensively discussed in the literature on optimization and machine learning [Miettinen, 1999; Bishop, 2006]. In addition to model combination methods, another important issue is how to collect or construct multiple different reward models. One of the simplest approaches is to employ ensemble 7This problem is also called reward hacking or reward gaming [Krakovna et al., 2020; Skalse et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2022], which refers to the phenomenon where the agent attempts to trick the reward model but fails to align its actions with the true intended objectives of the task. Imagine student who is assigned homework and is rewarded with points or praise for completing it. The student might then find ways to finish the homework with minimal effort to maximize the reward, such as copying and pasting solutions from the internet or previous assignments, rather than solving the problems themselves. 4.4 Improved Human Preference Alignment 193 learning techniques, such as developing diverse reward models from different subsets of given dataset or from various data sources. For RLHF, it is also possible to construct reward models based on considerations of different aspects of alignment. For example, we can develop reward model to evaluate the factual accuracy of the output and another reward model to evaluate the completeness of the output. These two models are complementary to each other, and can be combined to improve the overall evaluation of the output. Another approach is to employ different off-the-shelf LLMs as reward models. This approach is simple and practical, as many strong pretrained LLMs are readily available and we just need to use them with little or no modification. This raises an interesting question: can an LLM that aligns with other LLMs outperform those LLMs? Probably not at first glance. Intuitively, one might assume that target LLM merely imitating other LLMs based on limited supervision would struggle to fully capture the nuanced behaviors of its supervisors. However, given the strong generalization ability of LLMs, this approach can, in fact, be quite beneficial. For example, using open-source or commercial LLMs as reward models has demonstrated strong performance in aligning LLMs, even achieving state-of-the-art results on several popular tasks [Lambert et al., 2024].

sections.title: 4.4.2 Direct Preference Optimization
sections.content: Although learning reward models is standard step in reinforcement learning, it makes the entire training process much more complex than standard supervised training. Training reliable reward model is itself not an easy task, and poorly trained reward model can greatly affect the outcome of policy learning. We now consider an alternative alignment method, called direct preference optimization (DPO), which simplifies the training framework by eliminating the need to explicitly model rewards [Rafailov et al., 2024]. This method directly optimizes the policy based on user preferences, rather than training separate reward model. As result, we can achieve human preference alignment in supervised learning-like fashion. Figure 4.10 shows comparison of the standard RLHF method and the DPO method. Before deriving the DPO objective, let us first review the objective of policy training used in RLHF. As discussed in Section 4.3.3, the policy is typically trained by optimizing loss function with penalty term. The DPO method assumes simple loss function where the quality of the output given the input is evaluated by the reward model r(x, y). But it should be noted that the loss function here depends on the parameters of the policy (i.e., θ) rather than the parameters of the reward model (i.e., ϕ). The main advantage of DPO lies in its simplicity and efficiency. The DPO objective is very straightforward it directly optimizes for preference-based feedback, rather than relying on separately developed reward models. Moreover, DPO is generally more sample-efficient, as it learns from fixed dataset without the need for the computationally expensive sampling process used in PPO. This makes DPO popular method for human preference alignment, especially when developing and applying reward models via reinforcement learning is challenging. DPO can broadly be viewed as an offline reinforcement learning method, where the training data is pre-collected and fixed, and there is no exploration. In contrast, online reinforcement learning methods like PPO, which require exploring new states through interaction with the environment (using the reward model as proxy), also have their unique advantages. One of the benefits of online reinforcement learning is that it allows the agent to continuously adapt to changes in the environment by learning from real-time feedback. This means that, unlike offline methods, online methods are not constrained by the static nature of pre-collected data and can discover new problem-solving strategies. In addition, exploration can help the agent cover wider range of state-action pairs, thus improving generalization. This could be an important advantage for LLMs, as generalization is considered critical aspect in applying such large models.

sections.title: 4.4.3 Automatic Preference Data Generation
sections.content: Although learning from human preferences is an effective and popular method for aligning LLMs, annotating preference data is costly. Learning from human feedback not only suffers from limited scalability, but may also introduce bias because human feedback is inherently subjective. As result, one can turn to AI feedback methods to address these scalability and consistency issues without the limitations associated with human annotators. As with data generation for instruction fine-tuning, generating preference data using LLMs is straightforward. Given set of inputs, we first use an LLM to generate pairs of outputs. Then, we prompt the LLM to determine the preferred output for each pair, given the corresponding input. Below is an example of prompting the LLM to generate preference label for pair of consumer service responses. 4.4 Improved Human Preference Alignment 197 Consider customer service scenario where customer poses request. You will review two responses to this request. Please indicate which response is preferred. Note that good response should be courteous, clear, and concise. It should address the customers concern directly, provide helpful information or solution, and maintain positive tone. Request: Hello, noticed that my order hasnt arrived yet, though it was scheduled to arrive several days ago. Could you please update me on its status? Thank you! Response A: Im very sorry for the delay and understand how disappointing this can be. Were doing our best to sort this out quickly for you. Response B: Hey, stuff happens! Your package will get there when it gets there, no need to stress. Response is preferred. Once we collect such preference labels, we can use them, along with the input and two responses, to train the reward model. We can, of course, consider providing few demonstrations or using sophisticated prompting techniques, such as CoT, to improve labeling performance. For example, we can include in the prompt an example showing how and why one of the two responses is preferred based on CoT rationale. In addition to preference labels, we can also obtain the probability associated with each label [Lee et al., 2023]. simple method is to extract the probabilities for the label tokens, such as and B, from the probabilities output by the LLM. We can then use the Softmax function or other normalization techniques to re-normalize these probabilities into distribution over the labels. These probabilities of preferred labels can serve as pointwise supervision signals for training the reward model, as discussed in Section 4.4.1. While scaling up AI data generation is easy, ensuring its accuracy and diversity remains crucial. Here, the data quality and diversity issues involve not only the labeling of preferences but also the inputs and outputs of the model. Therefore, we often need to use variety of techniques to obtain large-scale, high-quality data. For example, one can generate diverse model outputs and annotations by using different LLMs, prompts, in-context demonstrations, and so on [Cui et al., 2024]. Dubois et al. [2024] report that the variability in pairwise preference data is important for training LLMs from either human or AI feedback. While learning from AI feedback is highly scalable and generally more consistent than human feedback, this method is more suited to well-defined tasks where objective performance metrics are available. By contrast, learning from human feedback is more advantageous when aligning AI systems with human values, preferences, and complex real-world tasks that require understanding of subtle or subjective context. These methods can be combined to train LLMs that benefit from both human insights and the scalability of AI feedback. 198 Alignment

sections.title: 4.4.4 Step-by-step Alignment
sections.content: So far, our discussion of alignment has primarily focused on the use of reward models for evaluating entire input-output sequence pairs. These methods can be easily adapted to scenarios where the correctness of the output can be verified based on the final answer. For example, in the task of calculating mathematical expression, reward model can provide positive feedback if the answer is correct, and negative feedback if the answer is wrong. However, in many problems that require complex reasoning, simply examining the correctness of the final result is insufficient for learning. Imagine student who is only given the final answer to challenging math problem. Knowing whether the final answer is right or wrong does not help the student figure out where they went wrong and how to calculate the correct answer. better approach would be to guide the student with step-by-step breakdown of the problem-solving process and help the student understand the underlying concepts and logic behind these steps. In Chapter 3, we studied CoT methods to prompt LLMs to explicitly write out intermediate steps or the reasoning process needed to reach conclusion or solve problem. We saw that breaking down problem into smaller parts could make it easier to understand the solution path and increase the accuracy of the output. These methods can be naturally extended to the alignment of LLMs, that is, we supervise the model during the intermediate steps of reasoning. Consider reasoning task where an LLM produces sequence of reasoning steps = {y1, ..., yns} for the given input. The result of the reasoning is assumed to be contained in the last step yns, and can be easily verified. For this reasoning problem, Uesato et al. [2022] categorize LLM fine-tuning approaches into two classes: Outcome-based Approaches. Supervision occurs only when the end result is verified. This is standard method for learning from human feedback we have discussed in this chapter. For example, the LLM is optimized to maximize some form of the reward r(x, y). Process-based Approaches. Supervision is applied to all intermediate steps in addition to the last step. To do this, we need to develop reward model to give supervision signal at each step, and design loss functions that can make use of such supervision signals. Figure 4.11 shows two LLM outputs for an example math problem. Although the LLM gives the correct final answer in both cases, it makes mistakes during the problem-solving process in the second output. Outcome-based approaches overlook these mistakes and give positive feedback for the entire solution. By contrast, process-based approaches can take these mistakes into account and provide additional guidance on the detailed reasoning steps. key challenge for process-based approaches is that we need to get step-level feedback during (potentially) long reasoning path. We can collect or generate reasoning paths corresponding to problems from existing datasets. Human experts then annotate each step with correctness labels. These annotations can be used to directly train LLMs or as rewards in reward modeling. However, in practice, richer annotations are often employed [Lightman et al., 2024]. In addition to the correct and incorrect labels, step can also be labeled as neutral to indicate that while the step may be technically correct, it might still be problematic within the overall reasoning process. Furthermore, to improve the efficiency of data annotation, techniques such as active learning can be employed. Identifying obvious errors usually does not significantly contribute to learning from 4.4 Improved Human Preference Alignment 199 Question (from The International Junior Math Olympiad): Jessica has lot of apps on her phone. The number of apps she has is divisible by 5. If she downloaded 10 more apps, she would still have less than 50 apps. What is the maximum original number of apps Jessica could have? Response 1: Response 2: y1: must be multiple of 5, i.e., 0 (mod 5). y1: The number of apps is divisible by 5, so must be multiple of 5. y2: After downloading 10 apps, the total total number of apps should still be less than 50: + 10 < 50. Solving this inequality: < 40. y2: If she downloads 10 more apps, her new total will be + 10, and this must be less than 50. Therefore, + 10 < 50. Simplifying this gives < 40. Since must be multiple of 5 and less than 40, the largest value of is 35. y3: must be less than or equal to the largest multiple of 5, which is 40. problematic y3: y4: Verify the result. If = 35, then after downloading 10 apps, Jessica would have: 35 + 10 = 45 which satisfy 45 < 50. y5: The maximum original number of apps is 35. correct y4: But + 10 should not be more than or equal to 50. So we need to subtract 5 from 40. problematic y5: Therefore, the final result is 35. correct x Fig. 4.11: Two LLM responses to math problem. In response 1, both the final result and all the reasoning steps are correct. In response 2, the final result is correct, but there are mistakes in the reasoning process (highlighted in red). For outcome-based approaches, both responses are considered correct. For process-based approaches, the mistakes in response 2 can be considered in reward modeling. reasoning mistakes. Instead, annotating steps that the model confidently considers correct but are actually problematic is often more effective. Given set of step-level annotated reasoning paths and corresponding inputs, we can train reward model to provide feedback for supervising policy learning. The reward model can be treated as classification model, and so its architecture can be Transformer decoder with Softmax layer stacked on top. At step k, the reward model takes both the problem description (denoted by x) and the reasoning steps generated so far (denoted by yk) as input and outputs probability distribution over the label set {correct, incorrect} or {correct, incorrect, neutral}. Then the learned reward model is used to evaluate reasoning paths by assessing the correctness of each step. simple method to model correctness is to count the number of steps that are classified as correct, given by r(x, y) = nsX k=1 δ(correct, C(x, yk)), (4.83) where C(x, yk) denotes the label with the maximum probability. We can also use log-probabilities 200 Alignment of classification to define the reward of the entire path r(x, y) = nsX k=1 log Pr(correctx, yk), (4.84) where Pr(correctx, yk) denotes the probability of the correct label generated by the reward model. The reward score r(x, y) can then be used to train the policy in RLHF as usual. While we restrict our discussion to math problems, the approaches described here are general and can be applied to wide variety of tasks that involve multi-step reasoning and decisionmaking. Moreover, we can consider various aspects when assessing the quality of step, rather than just its correctness. For example, in dialogue systems, responses must not only be accurate but also contextually appropriate across multiple turns of conversation. If model provides correct response but fails to maintain coherence in the context of the ongoing dialogue, steplevel feedback could help the model identify and correct such discrepancies. Also note that the process-based approaches are related to the fine-grained reward modeling approaches discussed in Section 4.4.1.3. All these approaches essentially aim to provide more detailed supervision to LLMs by breaking their outputs into smaller, more manageable steps. However, process-based feedback focuses more on evaluating the correctness of step based on its preceding steps, while the approaches in Section 4.4.1.3 emphasize evaluating each step independently. The idea of aligning LLMs step by step has great application potential, especially considering the recent shift towards more complex reasoning tasks in the use of LLMs. For example, both the GPT o1 and o3 models are designed with more advanced reasoning techniques (such as long internal CoT) to solve challenging problems like scientific and mathematical reasoning [OpenAI, 2024]. These tasks often rely on long and complex reasoning paths, and therefore, it seems essential to introduce detailed supervision signals in the reasoning process. Moreover, from practical perspective, effective supervision on long reasoning paths not only improves reasoning performance, but also helps the model eliminate unnecessary reasoning steps, thereby reducing reasoning complexity and improving efficiency. 4.4.5 Inference-time Alignment So far in this section, we have explored variety of methods to align models with human preferences and annotations. However, one of the significant limitations of many such methods is that LLMs must be fine-tuned. For RLHF and its variants, training LLMs with reward models can be computationally expensive and unstable, leading to increased complexity and costs when applying these approaches. In this case, we can consider performing alignment at inference time, thus avoiding the additional complexity and effort involved. One simple way to achieve inference-time alignment is to use the reward model to select the best one from alternative outputs generated by the LLM, method known as Best-of-N sampling (BoN sampling). We can consider BoN sampling as form of reranking. In fact, reranking methods have been widely used in NLP tasks, such as machine translation, for long time. They are typically applied in situations where training complex models is costly. In such cases, directly reranking the outputs allows for the incorporation of these complex models at very low cost8. 8Reranking methods can also help us explore what are known as model errors and search errors, although these 4.5 Summary 201 In the BoN sampling process, the LLM takes the input sequence and generates different output sequences {ˆy1, ..., ˆyN }: {ˆy1, ..., ˆyN } = argTopN [Pr(yx)] , (4.85) where the argTopN operation returns the top-N outputs that maximize the function Pr(yx). These outputs can be generated in variety of ways, depending on the search algorithm used by the model (e.g., sampling or beam search). Once the -best output candidates are generated, the reward model is used to evaluate and select the best one: ˆybest = arg max ˆy{ˆy1,...,ˆyN } r(x, ˆy). (4.86) It is worth noting that the result of BoN sampling is also influenced by the diversity of the -best list. This is common issue with most reranking methods. Ideally, the -best output candidates should have relatively high quality but be sufficiently different from each other. In many text generation systems, the -best outputs are very similar, often differing by just one or two words. The diversity issue is even more challenging in LLMs, as the -best outputs generated by an LLM can differ in wording, yet their semantic meanings are often quite similar. In practice, one can adjust the model hyperparameters and/or use different LLMs to generate more diverse output candidates for reranking. Nevertheless, as with many practical systems, we need to make trade-off between selecting high-quality candidates and ensuring sufficient variation in the generated outputs. BoN sampling can be used for training LLMs as well. closely related method is rejection sampling. In this method, we first select the best outputs from the -best lists using the reward model, and then take these selected outputs to fine-tune the LLM. In this way, we can introduce human preferences into the training of LLMs using much simpler approach compared to RLHF. Many LLMs have adopted rejection sampling for fine-tuning [Nakano et al., 2021; Touvron et al., 2023b].

sections.title: 4.5 Summary
sections.content: In particular, we In this chapter, we have explored range of techniques for aligning LLMs. have discussed fine-tuning methods that enable LLMs to follow instructions and align them with human preferences. One of the benefits of fine-tuning LLMs is computational efficiency. Unlike pre-training based on large-scale neural network optimization, fine-tuning is post-training step and so is less computationally expensive. Moreover, it is better suited to address problems that are not easily solved in pre-training, such as human value alignment. The widespread attention to AI alignment has also led to surge of research papers on this topic, which makes it difficult to comprehensively cover all recent techniques. However, we have tried to provide relatively issues are not often discussed in the context of LLMs. For example, suppose we have an old model and new, more powerful model. We can use the new model to select the best output from the -best list of the old model as the oracle output. The performance difference between the oracle output and the top-1 output of the original -best list reflects the performance gain brought by the new model. If the performance gain is significant, we can say that the old model has more model errors. If the gain is small, it may indicate that the issue lies in search errors, as the best candidates were not found. 202 Alignment detailed introduction to the fundamental approaches to alignment, such as instruction fine-tuning and RLHF. While we have focused on LLM alignment techniques in this chapter, the term AI alignment is wide-ranging concept. It generally refers to the process of ensuring that the behavior of an AI system aligns with human values, goals, and expectations. The idea of AI alignment can be traced back to the early days of AI. widely cited description of AI alignment comes from an article by the mathematician and computer scientist Norbert Wiener [Wiener, 1960]. The quote is as follows If we use, to achieve our purposes, mechanical agency with whose operation we cannot efficiently interfere ... we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire. At that time, alignment was not yet central concern in AI research. But today, it greatly influences the design of various AI systems. For example, in robotics, alignment is critical to ensuring that autonomous robots safely interact with humans and their environments. In autonomous driving, cars must not only follow traffic laws but also make complex, real-time decisions that prioritize human safety, avoid accidents, and navigate ethical dilemmas. In current AI research, alignment is often approached by developing surrogate objective that is analogous to the true goal and steering the AI system towards this objective. However, designing the objective of AI alignment is very difficult. One reason is that human values are diverse and often context-dependent, making it difficult to distill them into single, universally applicable objective function. Also, the complexity of real-world environments, where values and goals often conflict or evolve over time, further complicates alignment efforts. Even if we could define an appropriate objective, AI systems may find unintended ways to achieve it, leading to misaligned outcomes that still technically satisfy the objective but in harmful or counterproductive way. These challenges continue to motivate AI research towards more aligned systems, either through developing new mechanisms for perceiving the world or more efficient and generalizable methods to adapt these systems to given tasks. More importantly, as AI systems become more powerful and intelligent, especially given that recent advances in LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities in dealing with many challenging problems, the need for AI alignment has become more urgent. Researchers have started to be concerned with AI safety and warn the community that they need to develop and release AI systems with great caution to prevent these systems from being misaligned [Russell, 2019; Bengio et al., 2024]. https://github.com/NiuTrans/NLPBook https://niutrans.github.io/NLPBook CHAPTER

sections.title: Inference
sections.content: Once we have pre-trained and fine-tuned an LLM, we can apply it to make predictions on new data. This process is called inference, in which the LLM computes the probabilities of possible outputs given an input, and selects the output that maximizes the probability. The inference problem is generally expressed in the following form: ˆy = arg max Pr(yx), (5.1) where is the input sequence, is possible output sequence, and ˆy is the best output sequence. This is perhaps one of the most widely used formulas in NLP, and dates back to the early days of speech recognition and machine translation systems based on probabilistic models. Although for some applications, such as predicting single token using very small language model, solving this optimization problem seems trivial, for most situations the computational challenges arise from both calculating Pr(yx) and performing the arg max operation. The problems we therefore wish to address in this chapter are: 1) computing the prediction probability efficiently given trained LLM, and 2) devising an efficient approximate search for ˆy. At high level, these are fundamental issues in artificial intelligence, which have been extensively studied. Thus, many well-established techniques can be directly applied, for example, one can use greedy search algorithms to implement an efficient inference system. On the other hand, model-specific optimizations, such as efficient attention models for Transformers, can be considered to further improve efficiency. But in many practical applications, we still need to make trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, by carefully combining various techniques. The importance of the inference problem in LLMs also lies in the fact that many application scenarios require processing extremely long sequences. Recent studies have found that incorporating additional prompts and contextual information, such as long chain-of-thought prompts, during inference can significantly improve the performance of LLMs. This provides new approach to scaling LLMs: better results can be achieved by increasing the compute at inference time. For instance, through inference-time scaling, OpenAI [2024]s o1 and DeepSeek [2025]s R1 systems have demonstrated impressive performance on complex reasoning and programming tasks. This, in turn, has encouraged the NLP field to focus more on the issue of efficient inference. In this chapter, we will introduce the basic concepts and algorithms of LLM inference, including the prefill-decode framework, search (decoding) algorithms, and evaluation metrics of inference performance. We will then present methods for improving the efficiency of LLM inference, covering range of techniques for speeding up the system and compressing the model. Finally, we will discuss inference-time scaling, which is considered an important application of inference optimization. 204 Inference

sections.title: 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding
sections.content: In this section, we present the prefill-decode framework, the most common approach for describing and implementing LLM inference processes. We first introduce the notation and background knowledge, and then describe the details of the framework, such as the decoding algorithms for LLM inference.

sections.title: 5.1.1 Preliminaries
sections.content: Although we have described LLMs many times in this book, we begin by briefly defining the notation to facilitate the subsequent discussion, and to make this chapter self-contained. x: The input token sequence. It can be viewed as the prompt, which includes instructions, user inputs, and any additional context intended as input to the LLM. comprises + 1 tokens, denoted by x0 xm, where x0 is the start symbol SOS. y: The output token sequence, also called the response to the input. comprises tokens, denoted by y1 yn. y<i: The output tokens that precede position i, that is, y<i = y1 yi1. Pr(yx): The probability of generating given using the LLM. If the LLM is parameterized by θ, we can write it as Prθ(yx). [x, y]: The concatenated token sequence of and y. That is, [x, y] = x0 xmy1 yn. Occasionally, we use the notation seqx,y to represent [x, y]. Pr([x, y]): The probability of generating the token sequence [x, y] using the LLM. As described in Eq. (5.1), the goal of LLM inference is to maximize Pr(yx). Modeling this conditional probability is common in NLP. At first glance, it may appear to be sequence-tosequence modeling problem, where we transform sequence into another using encoder-decoder models. However, we are not discussing sequence-to-sequence problems or encoder-decoder architectures. Instead, as discussed in earlier chapters, this modeling problem can be addressed using decoder-only models. To do this, we can interpret the log-scale probability log Pr(yx) as the difference between log Pr([x, y]) and log Pr(x): log Pr(yx) = log Pr([x, y]) log Pr(x), (5.2) where log Pr([x, y]) and log Pr(x) can be obtained by running the LLM on the sequences [x, y] and x, respectively. For example, we can calculate the probability of generating using the chain 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding rule: log Pr(x) = log Pr(x0 xm) = log (cid:2) Pr(x0) Pr(x1x0) Pr(xmx0 xm1)(cid:3) = log Pr(x0) } {z =0 + j= log Pr(xjx<j) = j=1 log Pr(xjx<j). (5.3) In other words, we calculate the token prediction log-probability at each position of x, and sum all these log-probabilities. Note that since x0 is the predefined start symbol, we omit its contribution here. In common implementations of LLMs, however, we do not need to compute the log-probability of the input sequence, but use the LLM to directly compute the log-probability of the output sequence in the following form: log Pr(yx) = i= log Pr(yix, y<i), (5.4) where and y<i together form the context for predicting yi. Following common notation in the literature, we write Pr(yix, y<i) as shorthand for Pr(yi[x, y<i]). Now, we have two sub-problems in addressing the inference issue described in Eq. (5.1): Model Computation: we model Pr(yix, y<i) and compute it in an efficient manner. Search: we find the optimal (or sub-optimal) output sequence in terms of log Pr(yx). The second sub-problem is classic issue in NLP. We will show in Section 5.1.3 that there are several well-studied algorithms that can be applied to efficiently search the space of possible output sequences. The first sub-problem requires language model to produce distribution over vocabulary given sequence of context tokens. We can do this by training Transformer decoder, which outputs the distribution: Pr(x, y<i) = Softmax(HWo)m+i = Dec([x, y<i]). (5.5) (5.6) Here Dec() produces sequence of representations, each corresponding to position of the input sequence. So, if we input [x, y<i] to the LLM, is an matrix, where is the dimensionality of each representation, and = + is the number of context tokens. We can then use Softmax layer to transform these representations into distributions of tokens. Wo RdV is the linear mapping matrix of the Softmax layer, and HWo transforms the d-dimensional representations in into the -dimensional representations. The use of the subscript + indicates that the Softmax operation is applied only to the representation at position + i. See Figure 5.1 for an illustration of this architecture. 206 Inference Pr(x) Pr(x, y1) Pr(x, y<i) decoder output Self-attention Softmax Layer FFN Linear Mapping Embedding Layer layers x0 x1 xm y1 yi1 Fig. 5.1: The decoder-only architecture for LLMs. The decoder consists of an embedding layer and stack of Transformer layers. In each Transformer layer, the input passes through self-attention module followed by an FFN. The output of the decoder is sequence of representations that are taken as input to Softmax layer, which generates distribution of tokens for each position. Dec() is Transformer decoding network that consists of an embedding network and number of stacked self-attention and FFN networks. We will not discuss Transformers in detail here, as readers can easily learn about these models from the literature. However, it is worth pointing out that the difficulty of inference is in part from the use of the self-attention mechanism in Transformers. Recall that general form of single-head self-attention is given by: Attqkv(qi, K, V) = Softmax( qiK )V, (5.7) where qi Rd is the query at the position (i.e., position of yi ), and and Rid are the keys and values up to i, respectively. At each step during inference, we call the self-attention function Attqkv(), followed by an FFN, to generate d-dimensional representation that integrates information from both the current token and its left context. This process is repeated through layers of self-attention and FFN, forming stack of Transformer layers. The output of the L-th layer in this stack is the final representation. Each time, the model attends position to all previous positions, which results in 2i vector products (i times for qiK and times for the product of Softmax( qi ) and V). Hence, generating sequence of length len has time complexity of O(Ldlen2) for the self-attention network. Clearly, the inference of this model is slow for long sequences due to its quadratic time complexity with respect to sequence length. Therefore, many improvements to Transformers and alternative models have focused on efficient methods that are faster than this quadratic time complexity, such as sparse attention mechanisms and linear-time models. detailed discussion of efficient Transformers can be found in the previous chapters, and this section will focus on the 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding 207 standard Transformer architecture. Note that in self-attention, the queries, keys, and values of layer are linear mappings from the same input (i.e., the output of the previous layer). Once new key-value pair is generated, it is repeatedly used in subsequent inference steps. Rather than regenerating these key-value pairs during inference, more desirable way is to store them in structure, called the key-value cache, or the KV cache. Thus, (K, V) can naturally be viewed as KV cache. This cache is updated as follows: = Append(K, ki), = Append(V, vi), (5.8) (5.9) where (ki, vi) is the newly generated key-value pair at position i, and Append(a, b) denotes function that appends row vector to matrix a. Figure 5.2 shows how Transformer decoder works with KV cache. Finally, the process of computing log Pr(yx) is summarized as follows: 1. We concatenate and into sequence [x, y]. For each position of this sequence, we perform the following steps. (a) We compute the embedding of the token at position i, and feed the resulting embedding as an initial representation into the stack of Transformer layers. (b) In each Transformer layer, we pass the input representation through the self-attention network first and then through an FFN. In the self-attention network, the input representation is transformed into qi, ki, and vi. Then, we update the KV cache (K, V) using ki and vi (see Eqs. (5.8-5.9)). Then, we compute the output of the attention model by attending qi to (K, V) (see Eq. (5.7)). (c) If > (i.e., = 1), we take the output of the Transformer stack and compute the token prediction probability Pr(yix, y<i) via the Softmax layer (see Eq. (5.5)). 2. When reaching the end of the sequence, we obtain log Pr(yx) by summing log Pr(yix, y<i) over [1, n] (see Eq. (5.4)).

sections.title: 5.1.2 A Two-phase Framework
sections.content: As we have seen, language modeling is standard autoregressive process, where each token is generated one at time, conditioned on the previous tokens. For Transformers, this requires the model to maintain KV cache that stores past representations, and allows the newly generated representation to attend to this KV cache. When viewed from the perspective of KV-cache computation, LLM inference naturally divides into two phases: Prefilling. The prefilling phase initializes the KV cache for the input sequence x. It is called prefilling because the model prepares and stores the key-value pairs for each token in the 208 Inference attention v1 k2 v2 ki1 vi1 ki vi KV Cache (positions 1 to 1) qi query value key vi ki Linear maps Input Input at position (a) Updating the KV Cache at Position attention k1 v1 v2 ki1 vi1 ki vi ki+1 vi+1 KV Cache (positions 1 to i) qi+1 query value key vi+1 ki+1 Linear maps Input Input at position + (b) Updating the KV Cache at Position + 1 Fig. 5.2: Illustration of the KV cache. We update the KV cache at position, perform the attention operation, and then move to the next position to repeat the process. input before the actual token generation begins. The process of prefilling in an LLM can be expressed as: cache = Deckv(x), (5.10) where Deckv() is the decoding network (i.e., the same as Dec()), but it returns the KV 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding 209 cache in self-attention instead of the output representations. cache is list, given by: cache = {cache1, , cacheL}, (5.11) where cachel represents the key-value pairs for the l-th layer. Decoding. The decoding phase continues generating tokens based on the KV cache, as illustrated in Figure 5.2. When new token is input into the decoder, we update the KV cache in each layer by adding the new key-value pair. The updated cache is then used for self-attention computation. The token generation stops when some stopping criterion is met, such as when the generated token is the end symbol. The goal of decoding is to find the best predicted sequence, which is given by: ˆy = arg max Pr(ycache). (5.12) Although the probabilistic model is still conditioned on x, the decoding process operates on the KV cache computed from x. Thus we use Pr(ycache) instead of Pr(yx) to emphasize reliance on the KV cache. The prefilling and decoding processes are illustrated in Figure 5.3. Note that both processes share the same underlying autoregressive model. However, as shown in Table 5.1, they differ in several aspects, which lead to very different implementations in practice. In essence, although prefilling is still based on autoregressive token prediction, it can be considered an encoding process. This is because our goal is not to generate tokens, but to build context representation (i.e., the KV cache) for the subsequent steps in the decoding phase. In this sense, it shares some similarities with encoder-based models such as BERT, where we encode the input sequence into sequence of contextualized token representations. On the other hand, unlike BERT which generates bidirectional sequence representations, prefilling is based on standard language modeling tasks, and is thus unidirectional. Note that, since the entire sequence is input into the model all at once, all queries can be packed together and the self-attention operation is performed on in parallel. Let be the queries that are packed into one matrix. The self-attention model in prefilling can be defined as: Attqkv(Q, K, V) = Softmax( QK + Mask)V, (5.13) where Q, K, R(m+1)d. Mask R(m+1)(m+1) is mask that ensures that each token only attends to itself and the tokens that precede it in the sequence. It is represented by setting the values in the mask corresponding to future tokens to large negative number, for example, for the query qi and the key kj, we set the value of the entry (i, j) to if < j. One advantage of processing the sequence with single self-attention computation is that we can make better use of the parallel computing capabilities of modern GPUs, and so speed up prefilling. In general, the prefilling process is considered compute-bound. This is because merging multiple computational operations into one operation reduces the number of data transfers and the performance bottleneck usually comes from the computational capacity rather than memory bandwidth. Decoding is standard left-to-right text generation process. The token sequence is generated 210 Inference Transformer Decoder a n i t - S queries q0 keys values k0 q1 k1 v1 qm1 km1 vm1 Embedding Layer x0 x1 xm1 Processed all at once (a) Prefilling Pr(y1x) Pr(y2x, y1) Pr(ynx, y<n) Softmax Layer Transformer Decoder a n i t - S queries qm qm+1 keys values k0 v0 k1 v1 km1 vm1 km vm km+1 vm+1 qm+n km+n vm+n Embedding Layer xm y1 yn1 Processed step by step (n steps) (b) Decoding (at the n-th step) Fig. 5.3: Illustration of the prefilling and decoding processes. In prefilling, the entire input sequence is processed together and the KV cache is filled. In decoding, the LLM generates the output sequence step by step based on the prefilled KV cache. autoregressively by predicting one token at time based on the KV cache. Each newly generated token needs to attend to all previous tokens, following Eq. (5.7). Therefore, the decoding process is memory-bound due to its frequent access to the KV cache. The cost of decoding grows significantly as more tokens are generated. In most cases, decoding is computationally more expensive 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding 211 Prefilling Set up initial context x. Note that this is not just because, in decoding, the LLM generates tokens one by one and repeatedly updates the KV cache. As we will see in the following subsection, we may need to explore multiple different token sequences during decoding, which makes the problem more complex and increases its cost further.

sections.title: 5.1.3 Decoding Algorithms
sections.content: So far our discussion of LLM inference has primarily focused on the model computation problem, that is, how to compute Pr(yx). Now we turn to the discussion of the search problem. The problem can be stated as: given an LLM Pr(yx), how do we efficiently generate high-quality output sequence ˆy given the input sequence x? Naively, we can consider all of the output sequences, compute the prediction probability for each, and then select the output sequence having the highest probability. This method can guarantee the globally optimal solution, but direct exhaustive search is impractical for LLMs as the number of possible output sequences grows exponentially with the length of y. In practice, various heuristic search algorithms, such as greedy search and sampling-based search, are commonly employed to approximate the solution. Each of these methods offers tradeoffs between search quality and computational efficiency. The search problem, therefore, becomes balancing act between exploration and exploitation, where the goal is to find an efficient strategy that produces high-quality outputs without exploring the entire space. Before giving more detailed discussion of these methods, let us first informally define what search space is and how it is represented. In LLM inference, we define hypothesis as tuple of input and output sequences. Since is fixed during inference, we can simply consider each hypothesis as an output sequence. The search space, denoted by Y, is then the set of all possible hypotheses (i.e., output sequences) that the model can generate. The search problem for LLM inference can be re-expressed as: ˆy = arg max Pr(yx). yY (5.14) 212 Inference Path: node 0 node 3 node 9 node 11 node 17 Output: cats are playful. Probability: node 0 0 node 3 log Pr("cats"x) node 9 log Pr("are"x, "cats") node 11 log Pr("playful"x, "cats are") node 17 log Pr("."x, "cats are playful") root 1 2 3 4 playful . cats are is 7 8 9 10 playful . cats are is 16 17 19 20 playful . cats are is 11 12 13 14 playful . cats are is Fig. 5.4: search tree for decoding. At each node, we expand the tree by considering all possible tokens, each leading to new node representing potential continuation of the text. Here we highlight path through nodes 0, 3, 9, 11, and 17. The path represents the output sequence cats are playful., whose log-probability can be computed by accumulating the log-probabilities of these nodes. In NLP, is commonly represented in tree data structure to facilitate search. Figure 5.4 shows an example of the search tree resulting from small vocabulary. In this example, node represents prefix sequence that can be shared by many sequences. The search begins at the root of the tree, which can be regarded as the beginning of all sequences that can be generated1. Each child node extends the prefix of its parent node by adding one token from the vocabulary to the sequence, along with the probability of predicting the token given the prefix. This process continues as each node further branches out into additional child nodes, each representing new possible extension of the sequence with another token. The search tree thus grows deeper and wider, representing an exponentially growing number of potential sequences as more tokens are appended. This structure allows us to efficiently traverse through possible sequences, evaluating each in terms of the log-probability accumulated over the path from the root to that node. For example, in Figure 5.4, the path from the root to the node 17 corresponds to the output sequence Cats are playful.. The prediction log-probability log Pr(yx) is the sum of the log-probabilities of all the nodes on this path. In general, the search tree is organized into levels, where each level consists of all nodes at the same depth. Thus, the tree can be viewed as being expanded level by level, where each level corresponds to one decoding step. As the search progresses, new tokens are appended to these sequences, expanding them incrementally. Let Yi be the set of the sequences that the LLM generates at step i. Yi can be obtained by expanding each sequence in Yi1 with all possible next tokens in the vocabulary , given in the 1Here, since the predictions in LLMs are based on x, we can think of the root as representation of x. 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding following recursive form: Yi = Yi1 V, 213 (5.15) where Yi1 denotes the Cartesian product of Yi1 and (i.e., each sequence in Yi1 is concatenated with each token in ). Note that if sequence in Yi1 is complete (e.g., ending with the EOS token), it will not be expanded any further. Let Ψ(Yi) be the set of all complete sequences in Yi. Then, the search space can be expressed as: = Ψ(Y1) [ Ψ(Y2) [ [ Ψ(Ynmax), (5.16) where nmax is the maximum length of sequence. Most decoding algorithms follow this level-by-level search process. However, consists of an exponentially large number of sequences, and direct search in such vast space is computationally infeasible. Therefore, practical decoding algorithms often rely on strategies to prune the search space and avoid exploring low-quality sequences. For example, at each decoding step, Yi can be obtained in the following way: Yi = Prune(Yi1 ), (5.17) where Prune() is function that selectively removes sequences less likely to result in highquality outcomes. In general, we expect that Yi Yi1 . Thus we can drastically reduce the number of sequences under consideration at each step, ensuring that the computational load does not grow exponentially with the sequence length. Next, we will introduce these decoding algorithms. Some of them have already been discussed in sequence-to-sequence models, while others are more commonly used in LLMs.

sections.title: 5.1.3.1 Greedy Decoding
sections.content: Greedy search (or greedy decoding) is one of the most widely used decoding methods in NLP, particularly in text generation tasks like machine translation. The idea behind greedy search is straightforward: at each step in generation, it selects the next token that has the highest prediction probability. For each sequence = y1 yi Yi1 , we can evaluate it using log Pr(yx). This log-probability can be easily computed by noting that: log Pr(yx) = log Pr(y1 yix) log Pr(y<ix) } {z accumulated up to the parent node = + log Pr(yix, y<i) } {z newly computed for the current node , (5.18) Here the first term is the sum of the log-probabilities of the path from the root to the parent node, which has been computed in the previous decoding steps. At step i, we only need to compute the second term which is the standard token prediction log-probability produced by the LLM. 214 Inference The best token at step is then chosen as: ytop1 = arg max yiV = arg max yiV = arg max yiV log Pr(y1 yix) + log Pr(yix, y<i)(cid:3) (cid:2) log Pr(y<ix) {z } fixed wrt. yi log Pr(yix, y<i). Thus, the best sequence generated up to step is given by: ytop1 = y1 yi1ytop1 . Finally, Yi contains only this sequence: Yi = {ytop1}. (5.19) (5.20) (5.21) The greedy choice in one decoding step is illustrated in Figure 5.5 (a). Greedy search offers computational efficiency and is simple to implement. Its primary disadvantage, however, lies in its suboptimal nature high-quality sequences are likely pruned at early stages of decoding. Therefore, greedy search is appealing for tasks that demand speed and simplicity. For tasks that require better search results, alternative strategies such as beam search, which explores multiple potential paths simultaneously, are preferable.

sections.title: 5.1.3.2 Beam Decoding
sections.content: Beam search (or beam decoding) is natural extension of greedy search. Instead of retaining only the single most probable sequence at each step, beam search maintains fixed number of the best candidate sequences, known as the beam width K. See Figure 5.5 (b) for an illustration. Unlike greedy search, which only expands one parent node, beam search considers extensions from all sequences stored in Yi1. At step i, we evaluate all possible continuations by computing the full sequence log-probabilities for the set Yi1 . The top sequences with the highest accumulated probabilities are then selected to form Yi: Yi = {ytop1, , ytopK} = argTopK yYi1V log Pr(yx), (5.22) where argTopK is function that ranks the probabilities of all evaluated sequences and returns the top candidates. Adjusting the beam width allows us to balance search efficiency and accuracy. While larger beam explores wider search space, the performance gains often diminish. In practical LLM inference, relatively small beam width, such as = 2 to = 5, is usually sufficient to achieve high-quality generation. Note that while beam search has historically played an important role in sequence generation tasks such as machine translation, sampling-based decoding methods are now more commonly used in open-ended LLM text generation because they produce more diverse and flexible outputs. 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding 215 4 is is 4 is 4 is ① Expansion ② Ranking ③ Output (1-best) 5 6 7 9 . cute on are sick 6 7 9 8 5 cute Pr = .34 ok 6= cute on Pr = . pruned sick Pr = .21 pruned are Pr = . pruned . sections.title: 5.1.3.3 Sampling-based Decoding
sections.content: Both greedy and beam search generate deterministic outputs, that is, given an LLM, the output of the model will always be the same every time it processes the same input. The deterministic nature 216 Inference of greedy and beam search ensures predictability and reliability in applications where consistent outcomes are critical, such as in formal document generation, where varying outputs could cause confusion or errors. On the other hand, one disadvantage of these methods is the lack of diversity and flexibility. For example, in creative tasks like story generation or conversational agents, generic or repetitive outputs generated by deterministic systems are often less engaging. To introduce variation into LLM outputs, we can use sampling-based decoding methods. There are two commonly used methods. Top-k Sampling. This method selects the next token from the top-k most likely candidates at each step of the generation process [Fan et al., 2018]. Let be the selection pool for top-k sampling. We can define it as: = {ytop1 , , ytopk }, (5.23) , , ytopk where {ytop1 } are the top-k tokens selected based on their prediction probabilities (see Eq. (5.22)). Once the selection pool is determined, we renormalize the probability distribution over i. One of the simplest ways to do this is to renormalize their probabilities: Pr(yix, y<i) = Pr(yix, y<i) yj Pr(yjx, y<i) . (5.24) Alternatively, we can calculate the distribution by using the Softmax function: Pr(yix, y<i) = exp(uyi) yj exp(uyj ) , where uyi is the logit for token yi. Then, we sample token yi from this distribution: yi Pr(yix, y<i). The corresponding sequence is = y1 yi1 yi, and Yi is given by: Yi = {y}. (5.25) (5.26) (5.27) Top-p Sampling. This sampling method, also known as nucleus sampling, follows procedure similar to that of top-k sampling. Instead of drawing from fixed size candidate pool, it selects the next token from the smallest set of tokens that together have cumulative probability higher than predefined threshold [Holtzman et al., 2020]. In this way we prevent the prediction from choosing from low-probability tokens in the long tail that could lead to incoherent or nonsensical outputs. To obtain the candidate pool in the top-p sampling method, we can sort all tokens by their predicted probabilities. Then, starting with the token with the highest probability, we continue to add tokens to the candidate pool until the cumulative probability of the tokens in the pool reaches or exceeds (we denote the size of the candidate pool at this point as kp). The candidate pool can then be expressed as: = {ytop1 , , ytopkp }. (5.28) 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding 217 (a) β = 0.1 (b) β = 0. (c) β = 2.0 Fig. 5.6: Histogram estimates of the distributions generated by the Softmax function with different values of the temperature parameter β. The subsequent steps, such as the renormalization of the distribution and sampling, are the same as in the top-k sampling method (see Eqs.(5.24-5.27)). See Figure 5.5 (c-d) for illustrations of the top-k and top-p sampling methods. By limiting the choices to smaller set of high-probability tokens, these methods strike balance between randomness and coherence. They allow for more diverse outputs while still maintaining reasonable level of relevance and fluency. However, the value of or must be carefully chosen: if or is too small, the output may still be overly deterministic (more like greedy decoding), and if or is too large, the LLM might produce degenerate outputs. In order to further control the randomness of the token selection process, the renormalized distribution Pr() is typically obtained by using the Softmax function with the temperature parameter, given by: Pr(yix, y<i) = exp(uyi/β) yj exp(uyj /β) , (5.29) Here β is temperature parameter that controls the sharpness of the probability distribution derived from logits. In Figure 5.6, we show simple examples involving distributions generated by the above function with different temperatures. When the temperature is set to higher value, the resulting probability distribution becomes more uniform, as the differences between the logits are diminished. This means that each token in the candidate pool has more equal chance of being selected, leading to greater diversity in the generated output. By contrast, when the temperature is set to lower value, the distribution becomes sharper, making the high-probability tokens even more likely to be chosen, which often results in more deterministic outputs. For example, if we set to 1 and β to very small number (approaching zero), the top-p sampling method will become equivalent to the greedy search method.

sections.title: 5.1.3.4 Decoding with Penalty Terms
sections.content: One common improvement to decoding methods in text generation is to modify the search objective. For example, one can replace maximum posteriori (MAP) decoding with minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding [Kumar and Byrne, 2004], where the focus shifts from selecting the single most probable output to choosing an output that minimizes the expected risk over distribution of possible outputs. Here we explore methods that incorporate penalty terms into decoding. These methods offer simple but effective way to make decoding more controllable. Recall from Eq. (5.14) that the goal of decoding is to maximize the likelihood of the output 218 Inference sequence. With penalty terms, the objective is extended to include additional factors that penalize certain behaviors in the generated text. general form of the new objective is given by: ˆy = arg max (cid:2) log Pr(yx) λ Penalty(x, y)(cid:3), (5.30) yY where Penalty(x, y) is function that quantifies the degree to which the generated sequence violates certain constraints or exhibits undesirable behaviors given the input x. The design of Penalty() is very flexible, thus allowing us to incorporate wide range of constraints or prior knowledge into it. Below, we present some common types of penalty functions. Repetition Penalty. repetition penalty discourages the model from generating repetitive or redundant text. The penalty function might measure the frequency of repeated tokens or phrases in the generated sequence and impose penalty proportional to their occurrence. Length Penalty. length penalty ensures that the generated sequence adheres to desired length. For example, in text summarization tasks, the penalty function could penalize outputs that are too short or too long. Diversity Penalty. diversity penalty promotes variation in the generated text. For example, in beam search, we can measure the similarity between generated hypotheses, and encourage the model to explore different hypotheses. Constraint-based Penalty. constraint-based penalty enforces specific constraints related to the content or style of the generated text. For example, in machine translation, the penalty function could penalize outputs that deviate from desired tone or terminology. In general, we can consider Penalty(x, y) as function that defines the cost assigned to the generated sequence given the input sequence x. Alternatively, this function can be defined to assess the hidden states of an LLM when generating y. For example, Su et al. [2022] develop penalty term that calculates the maximum distance between the representation of the predicted token and the representations of the previously generated tokens. Therefore, the search objective will penalize degenerate outputs, such as text with many repetitions. The method described in Eq. (5.30) is general and can be easily adapted to different search algorithms. For example, in greedy search, we can keep the single sequence that maximizes log Pr(yx) λ Penalty(x, y) at each decoding step; in sampling-based search, we can rank and select the top-ranked sequences based on log Pr(yx) λ Penalty(x, y) to form the candidate pool.

sections.title: 5.1.3.5 Speculative Decoding
sections.content: Speculative decoding stems from the concept of speculative execution, where system makes educated guesses about future actions and performs them in advance. If the guess is correct, the results are immediately available, which speeds up processing. In the case of LLM inference, suppose we have two models. One is smaller, faster model (called the draft model), and the other is the full, stronger model (called the verification model). These two models represent two 5.1 Prefilling and Decoding 219 ends of the spectrum in LLM inference: the draft model is efficient but not very accurate; the verification model is usually the one we want to run, but it is very slow. Given prefix, we first use the draft model to speculatively predict sequence of likely future tokens. This is standard autoregressive decoding process, but it is still fast in practice due to the high efficiency of the draft model. Then, the verification model evaluates the speculated tokens in parallel. It checks whether the predicted tokens can be accepted under the verification model. Note that, since we can deal with these tokens all at once, the verification can be done in single step for all the tokens simultaneously, rather than in token-by-token manner. If the speculated tokens are correct, they are accepted, and the process continues with the next set of tokens. If they are incorrect, the incorrect speculations are discarded, and the verification model is used to generate new tokens. To be more specific, let us see the speculative decoding method presented in Leviathan et al. [2023]s work. In this method, the draft model is small language model, denoted by Prq(yix, y<i), while the verification model is the full LLM, denoted by Prp(yix, y<i). The goal is to use the draft model, given prefix, to autoregressively predict up to τ tokens. The verification model is then employed to generate the last token at the point where speculative predictions are rejected. Figure 5.7 illustrates one step in this decoding process. For simplicity, we describe the greedy version of speculative decoding. The speculative decoding algorithm can be summarized as follows. Given the prefix [x, yi], we use the draft model to predict the next τ consecutive tokens, denoted by {ˆyi+1, , ˆyi+τ }. This is token-by-token generation process, given by: ˆyi+t = arg max yi+t Prq(yi+tx, yi, ˆyi+1 ˆyi+t1). Note that we can compute these probabilities in parallel, and so this verification step is efficient. We determine the maximum number of accepted speculated tokens. To keep the notation uncluttered, we denote Prq(ˆyi+tx, yi, ˆyi+1 ˆyi+t1) and Prp(ˆyi+tx, yi, ˆyi+1 ˆyi+t1) simply by q(ˆyi+t) and p(ˆyi+t), respectively. We then define the acceptance rule as follows: if q(ˆyi+t) p(ˆyi+t), then we accept this speculation. By contrast, if q(ˆyi+t) > p(ˆyi+t), we reject this speculation with probability 1 p(ˆyi+t) q(ˆyi+t) .
