Subfigure (a) shows discriminative verifier which attaches classification head to the last hidden layer of the LLM to output numerical probability of correctness. Subfigure (b) shows generative verifier that prompts the LLM with the query z, reasoning history yt, and an instruction to generate natural language critique instead of scalar value. Here Pr() represents the probability distribution modeled by an existing LLM. Thus we can directly use strong LLMs to give accurate verification without training. Figure 6.1 compares this generative approach with traditional discriminative verifiers. While natural language critiques are useful for humans, some search algorithms (such as tree search) may require numerical scores to rank different reasoning paths. To extract continuous score from generative verifier, common method is to measure the probability of the model outputting an indicator token (such as Correct or Incorrect) as the very first word of its critique. Therefore, the numerical verification score can be defined as: v(z, yt, c) = Pr(yanchor = Correctz, yt, c). (6.14) Here yanchor is the indicator token that is typically extracted from the output text using heuristics. Generative verifiers have several advantages over traditional scalar reward models. First, they provide interpretability for problem solving. Because the verifier explains its reasoning in text, developers can diagnose why reasoning path is accepted or not. Second, they enable selfcorrection. Since the text critique often explicitly states how to fix mistake (like providing the correct expansion 2y + 4 in our example), the reasoning system can directly integrate this feedback to correct its current state and continue searching, rather than simply discarding the entire path. Third, they require minimal modification of the architecture. As long as current LLMs have strong reasoning capabilities, the exact same model can be used as both the problem solver and the verifier.

sections.title: 6.3.4.3 Formal Symbolic Systems as Verifiers
sections.content: While neural verifiers are widely used, they share common weakness: they are still neural networks. This means they can also hallucinate or make logical mistakes. For tasks that require strict precision, such as complex mathematics or software engineering, we can also use formal symbolic systems as verifiers. For example, in code optimization tasks, when model attempts 6.4 Learning to Reason 261 to optimize intermediate representation code (such as LLVM-IR), formal equivalency checker (such as Alive2) can automatically verify if the newly generated code maintains the exact same semantics as the original. Formal systems strictly follow pre-defined mathematical and logical rules, and so their judgments are 100% reliable. To use formal system as verifier, the LLM must generate its reasoning steps as executable code or formal mathematical statements rather than just plain natural language. For example, when solving math problem, the LLM might write small Python script to perform specific intermediate calculation. The system then executes this code using an external tool. The verification process is very straightforward: If the code runs without errors and produces valid output, the reasoning step is verified as correct. If the code throws an error (such as syntax error or math violation), the reasoning step is verified as incorrect. Formally, let an intermediate step yt be generated block of code or formal logic, and let represent the formal execution environment. The verification score can be defined as: v(x, y<t, yt) = 1, 0, if E(yt) returns the correct result, otherwise. (6.15) This approach has clear advantage: it eliminates the false positives caused by verifier hallucinations. Furthermore, when the execution fails, the formal system usually generates an error message. This error message can be fed back into the LLM to help the model understand what went wrong and correct its logic in the next attempt. However, using formal symbolic systems also comes with limitations. First, it requires the LLM to have strong coding or formalization skills, as translating abstract reasoning into strict code is difficult. Second, while formal systems are perfect for math and coding, they are not suitable for open-ended, real-world tasks (like writing an essay or planning trip) where reasoning cannot be easily mapped to rigid logical rules.

sections.title: 6.4 Learning to Reason
sections.content: Improving the reasoning capabilities of LLMs is challenging, and therefore generally requires combination of multiple methods. As discussed in the previous section, inference-time scaling aims to activate the thinking process of existing LLMs during generation. Alternatively, natural idea is to internalize these reasoning abilities directly into the model parameters during training. In this section, we will focus on this learning to reason paradigm. Reasoning data can be incorporated into any training phase. For example, during pre-training, reasoning paths can simply be added as normal text for standard next-token prediction. Also, we can consider reasoning-based training in the post-training phase. For example, during supervised fine-tuning, models can be fine-tuned on high-quality instances of step-by-step problem-solving. 262 Reasoning This is commonly achieved by training the model on datasets with CoT trajectories. Furthermore, reinforcement learning can be applied to further optimize these reasoning processes. Here we focus on incorporating reasoning-based supervision in LLM alignment. In the following subsections, we will discuss supervised reasoning data, process supervision, reinforcement learning techniques, and strategies for scaling reasoning capabilities.

sections.title: 6.4.1 Supervised Reasoning Data
sections.content: Formally, in supervised fine-tuning, an LLM is trained on dataset of input-output pairs = {(x, y)}. The standard training objective is ˆθ = arg max θ (x,y)D log Prθ(yx), (6.16) where Prθ() denotes the model parameterized by θ. If is simply the final conclusion, the model learns to predict the answer without explicitly generating the corresponding reasoning path. For reasoning-based training/tuning, we instead redefine as reasoning path. As shown in Eq. (6.2), we can represent the output as reasoning path consisting of sequence of reasoning steps = {y1, ..., ynp}. Thus, we can rewrite the above objective as ˆθ = arg max θ (x,{y1,...,ynp })D log Prθ(y1, ..., ynpx). (6.17) In this way, the model is explicitly provided with reasoning details and is trained to generate complete reasoning path, including the final conclusion. In practice, to separate the core reasoning process from other parts of the output, reasoning models often use special formatting tokens. widely adopted approach is to wrap the core reasoning steps inside <think> and </think> tags. When an LLM generates text using this format, the reasoning steps written inside the tags are referred to as CoT trace (or simply reasoning trace). We can think of this CoT trace as the scratchpad of the LLM. Just like student taking math exam who writes down intermediate calculations on scrap paper before writing the final answer on the official exam sheet, the LLM uses the <think> block to show its work. For example, training instance formatted with these tags might look like this: What is 15% of 80? <think> To calculate this easily, can break 15% down into 10% and 5%. First, 10% of 80 is 8. Next, 5% is half of 10%, which is 4. Adding them together: 8 + 4 = 12. </think> The answer is 12. Here the query is What is 15% of 80?. There are five steps in the output, where steps 1-4 6.4 Learning to Reason 263 represent the CoT trace and step 5 represents the conclusion. Both the <think> and </think> tags are valid tokens, and so the model will learn to generate them to indicate the core reasoning steps. On the user end, we can remove such tags to show clean output. Note that in practical applications, the output might be very complex and include content not related to reasoning. Therefore, introducing <think> and </think> tags can help the model concentrate on solving the reasoning problem. Reasoning data can also be represented using various other formats. One straightforward alternative is natural language step-by-step format. Instead of using special tokens, the data relies on text prefixes, such as Step 1:, Step 2:, or simply Thought: followed later by Answer:. Furthermore, reasoning data can be structured using role-based message separation. In modern chat templates, instead of mixing the reasoning and the answer in single message, the reasoning trace is assigned to an internal role (e.g., thought or system_scratchpad role), while the final conclusion is assigned to the standard assistant role. This separates the internal thinking of the LLM from the user-facing response at the system level.

sections.title: 6.4.2 Process Supervision
sections.content: As we discussed in Section 6.3.4, PRMs are powerful tools for verifying reasoning steps during inference. natural extension is to use it to guide the training of LLMs through process supervision. In standard outcome supervision (such as supervised fine-tuning), the model is only evaluated on the final outcome of the entire reasoning path y. If the model generates sequence of five steps and makes logical error in the third step, an outcome-based training approach might simply penalize the entire sequence. The model is left to guess which exact step caused the failure. This is known as the credit assignment problem [Minsky, 1961; Sutton, 1984]. Process supervision solves this by applying training signals at the step level. Instead of single reward for the whole path, the model receives feedback for every individual step yt. For example, imagine teaching student to solve complex algebra equation. If you only look at the final number they write down and say Wrong, the student does not know if they misunderstood the formula, made simple addition error, or forgot minus sign. Process supervision is like teacher pointing specifically to line 3 and saying Your logic broke down here. Process supervision is typically framed as reinforcement learning problem. To apply reinforcement learning to process supervision, we generally follow training loop of three steps: Rollout: The LLM receives an input and generates full reasoning path = {y1, . . . , ynp}. The rollout process can be repeated multiple times to generate set of reasoning paths Y. Verification: reward model (i.e., PRM checking intermediate steps) evaluates each path and returns reward score R(x, y). Update: reinforcement learning algorithm uses these rewards to update the model parameters θ.

sections.title: A simple training objective can be formalized as maximizing the expected reward
sections.content: J(θ) = EyPrθ(x) [R(x, y)] . (6.18) 264 Reasoning We can modify this objective to have more robust training, such as introducing the advantage function into the objective as in PPO. While this looks like standard reinforcement learning workflow used in general LLM alignment (as described in Chapter 4), there is fundamental difference in the nature of the reward. In typical LLM alignment tasks, the reward model usually evaluates the entire generated text and returns sparse reward at the very end. The reinforcement learning algorithm then struggles with the credit assignment problem, as it has to guess which tokens or segments actually contributed to that final score. In contrast, reasoning unfolds step-by-step. Therefore, the verification score, which we will denote as vt = v(x, yt) for simplicity, is inherently step-level signal. This characteristic makes reasoning tasks well-suited for modern reinforcement learning. Because vt is generated step by step, it naturally transforms sparse-reward language generation task into dense-reward environment. The main technical question then becomes how to properly transform these natural step-level scores vt into the formal training signals (such as structured step rewards rt or advantages At) required by the algorithms. Depending on the output format of the PRM and the reinforcement learning framework, we consider the following three methods.

sections.title: 6.4.2.1 Training with Binary Verification Scores
sections.content: In some cases, the PRM acts as strict rule checker (such as math calculator or code compiler). It simply returns binary score: vt {0, 1}. score of 1 means that the logic at step is correct given the previous steps, and 0 means that logical error occurs at this step. When dealing with binary scores, the idea is straightforward: single wrong step invalidates the entire reasoning path. If we want to assign sequence-level reward R(x, y) for the whole path, we can simply multiply all the step scores together R(x, y) = np t=1 vt. (6.19) Hence the model only gets positive reward if the verification score of every single step is 1. Alternatively, if the reinforcement learning algorithm supports step-level rewards (denoted as rt), we can penalize the model exactly where the failure happens. For example, we can give reward of 1 as long as the steps remain correct (vt = 1). The moment the model makes mistake (vt = 0), we assign negative reward and stop the generation.

sections.title: 6.4.2.2 Training with Real-valued Verification Scores
sections.content: In most neural PRMs, the verifier outputs continuous real number vt R. This could be probability from 0 to 1 (indicating the confidence that the reasoning path is correct) or an unnormalized scalar value. To apply continuous verification scores, the most common technique is reward shaping. Instead of using absolute scores, we define the immediate step reward rt as the marginal difference 6.4 Learning to Reason between the current step and the previous step: rt = vt vt1. (6.20) This method is very intuitive. Imagine PRM estimating the probability of getting the final answer right. If Step 1 has confidence of 0.4, and Step 2 contains brilliant deduction that raises the confidence to 0.9, the reward for Step 2 is r2 = 0.9 0.4 = +0.5. The model is rewarded for that specific logical leap. If Step 3 introduces calculation error and the confidence drops to 0.1, the reward is r3 = 0.1 0.9 = 0.8. When we sum these shaped rewards across the entire sequence, we have telescoping sum that forms our sequence-level reward R(x, y): R(x, y) = np t=1 rt = (v1 v0) + (v2 v1) + + (vnp vnp1) = vnp v0. (6.21) Here, v0 is generally assumed to be 0. In this derivation, the intermediate scores cancel out. This means that the overall sequence reward remains consistent with the evaluation of the final step. To understand how this step-by-step dense reward actually trains the model, we need to connect it to the reinforcement learning objective. As is shown in Eq. (6.18), our goal is to maximize the expected total reward over all possible generated paths. To make training efficient and have proper credit assignment, we typically use the principle of causality: an action taken at step can only affect the rewards received after this step. Therefore, rather than evaluating step using the entire sequence reward, we evaluate it using the future return Rt, which is defined as the sum of rewards from step to the end of the sequence: Rt = np k=t rk = vnp vt1. (6.22) Finally, we can train the model using the surrogate loss function L(θ) = np t=1 log Prθ(ytx, y<t) Rt. (6.23) This loss function provides step-level feedback mechanism. For any generated reasoning path, the model looks at the future return Rt at each step t. If Rt is positive, the loss function pushes the model to increase the probability log Prθ() of generating this step. If Rt is negative, it serves as penalty, which pushes the model to avoid generating this step in the future. 6.4.2.

sections.title: Incorporating Verification into the Advantage Function
sections.content: Many reinforcement learning algorithms (such as PPO) optimize the model using the advantage function At, which measures how much better an action was compared to what was expected. 266 Reasoning Instead of treating verification scores as raw rewards, we can incorporate them into the advantage calculation. One method is to introduce step-level verification into the temporal difference error. If the PRM is trained to estimate the expected future reward, we can treat it as the value baseline in standard actor-critic reinforcement learning. We calculate the advantage At using the temporal difference error At = rt + γvt vt1, (6.24) where rt is any external reward from the environment (usually 0 during intermediate thinking steps) and γ is the discount factor. Another method is to improve the design of the group relative advantage. In group relative policy optimization (GRPO), we dispense with absolute verification scores [Shao et al., 2024]. Instead, we compute the advantage by comparing group of reasoning paths. For an input x, the LLM generates group of different reasoning paths. verifier assigns score v(i) to the t-th step of the i-th path. The advantage A(i) is calculated by accumulating the standardized scores from step to the end of the path, as follows A(i) = n(i) k=t v(i) , (6.25) where n(i) as: is the total number of steps in the i-th path, and v(i) is the standardized score, defined v(i) = v(i) µ σ , (6.26) where µ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the scores across all steps of the paths in the group. For example, if model explores 5 different ways to solve an equation, and path #3 executes step that scores significantly higher than the average of all steps in these paths, path #3 receives positive advantage. Here, the group average µ serves as the baseline, which removes the need to train and run separate value network. Once the advantage At (or A(i) ) is calculated using either of these methods, it can be used as the scaling weight in the loss function. simplified version of the advantage-based loss function can be written as2: L(θ) = np t=1 log Prθ(ytx, y<t) At. (6.27) Note that the benefit of using the advantage At over the raw return Rt is variance reduction. By subtracting baseline, whether it is an estimated value vt1 or group average µ, the advantage function provides relative performance measure. It tells the model not just whether reasoning step is logically sound, but whether it is better than expected. This relative feedback prevents the 2Note that advanced algorithms like PPO and GRPO usually enhance this objective by adding clipping mechanism (restricting the probability ratio between the new and old policies) to prevent the model parameters from changing too drastically in single update. However, the core mathematical principle remains the same. 6.4 Learning to Reason 267 model from being overwhelmed by queries that are too easy or too hard.

sections.title: 6.4.3 On-Policy Distillation for Reasoning
sections.content: While process supervision provides step-by-step reward signals to guide reasoning, it still relies on scalar value to tell the model how well it is doing. To provide an even richer training signal, we can employ on-policy distillation (OPD). This method is generally used in post-training of LLMs, and aligns well with the goal of step-based supervision: making the training signals as dense as possible. Standard knowledge distillation can be viewed as kind of off-policy distillation. smaller student model learns by mimicking the reasoning paths generated by stronger teacher model. The student is trained on fixed dataset of these pre-recorded paths. However, reasoning is long and fragile process. If the student makes small mistake or chooses slightly different valid approach during actual generation, it enters state it has never seen in the training data. Because the student does not know how to recover from its mistakes, the reasoning process may collapse. This phenomenon is known as exposure bias or distribution shift. The core idea of OPD is that the student model learns from its own generated trajectories, rather than from trajectories sampled from the teacher model. Formally, let the teacher model be Prt() and the student model (parameterized with θ) be Prs θ(). The typical procedure of OPD consists of two steps: Student Rollout. Given an input x, the student model uses its current parameters θ to generate reasoning path = {y1, . . . , ynp}. Because the student generates this path itself, it naturally explores its own reasoning behaviors. This includes making slight deviations, taking alternative approaches, or even making mistakes that teacher would never make. Teacher Guidance. We then feed this student-generated path to the teacher model. At each step t, instead of providing scalar reward, the teacher model calculates the probability distribution for the next step Prt(x, y<t). Ideally, the student model is updated to align its step-level probability distribution with the distribution generated by the teacher model. The objective is to minimize the expected KL divergence between the two distributions over the reasoning paths generated by the student model: Lstep(θ) = EyPrs θ(x) " np t=

Because reasoning step yt typically consists of multiple tokens, the probability distribution over all possible multi-token steps resides in an exponentially large space. To address this, we fall back to the standard OPD approach, which operates at the token level. By treating the generated reasoning path as token sequence = {y1, . . . , yn}, the objective is 268 Reasoning reformulated to compute the KL divergence token by token over the vocabulary: Ltoken(θ) = EyPrs θ(x) DKL (cid:16) Prs (cid:17) θ(x, y<i) Prt(x, y<i) # . For given input x, we simply perform rollout to generate one (or small batch of) reasoning paths from the student model, and calculate the token-level KL divergence on these sampled rollouts. Figure 6.2 compares OPD with supervised fine-tuning and process supervision. To further understand the difference among these methods, imagine student trying to solve complex geometry problem: Supervised Fine-tuning. This is like giving the student textbook filled with the correct solutions written by the teacher to memorize. If the student decides to draw an auxiliary line differently than the textbook did, the textbook offers no help on how to proceed from that new starting point. Process Supervision (RL with PRMs). This is like having strict grader who checks the students work step-by-step and says, +1 point for step 1, and -1 point for step 2. It tells the student where they went wrong, but not how to fix it or what the correct next step should be. On-Policy Distillation. This is like having an expert tutor sitting right next to the student. When the student draws that unusual auxiliary line (a state not in the standard textbook), the tutor looks at the students current state and says, Okay, since you drew the line here, your next best step is to calculate this specific angle. Because the supervision of OPD comes in the form of full probability distribution over the vocabulary, the student receives very dense and rich learning signal. It learns not only what the single best next step is, but also the probabilities of other valid alternatives. This rich feedback is well suited for reasoning because it teaches the student model how to recover from deviations and maintain logical consistency across the entire output sequence, rather than just treating rationale as an isolated component. However, applying on-policy distillation comes with high computational cost. The process requires running large teacher model alongside the student during training to calculate probability distributions in real time. This is more expensive than standard off-policy distillation, where the outputs of the teacher model are only generated once and stored in static dataset.

Here, we briefly discuss several key aspects of scaling training for reasoning LLMs: large-scale reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, and long-context scaling. 6.4 Learning to Reason 269 Human/ Teacher Annotate/Generate This cat is cute . sections.title: 6.4.4.1 Large-scale Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: Reinforcement learning has become primary approach to improving the System 2 reasoning abilities of LLMs. For example, the success of many powerful reasoning models comes from scaling up reinforcement learning rather than using supervised fine-tuning only. An interesting phenomenon observed during large-scale reinforcement learning-based training is the emergence of the aha moment [DeepSeek, 2025]. Without explicit human annotation, LLMs learn to pause, recognize when they have made mistake, or even backtrack to try different approach. These abilities are difficult to elicit when relying solely on limited labeled data and standard supervised 270 Reasoning training. As training compute scales, the model can allocate longer CoT traces to harder problems, and thus discover how to think deeply on its own [Snell et al., 2024]. Recent large-scale empirical studies have demonstrated that the relationship between reinforcement learning compute and reasoning performance can be modeled by an S-shaped curve [Khatri et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2026]. key finding from this scaling law is that different training choices impact the curve differently. For instance, increasing the base capabilities of the LLM (e.g., using larger architectures or MoEs) and expanding the context window length can increase the performance limit. Conversely, algorithmic improvements, such as changing the loss function or adjusting advantage normalization, mainly make better use of the available compute budget but do not significantly improve the final performance. Scaling reinforcement learning is difficult. First, the computational cost is very high. For every training sample, the system generally performs rollout (running the model for inference) and then calls an extra reward model or another LLM to evaluate the generated output. When the number of training samples increases, this cost becomes significantly higher than that of standard supervised fine-tuning. This computational burden also makes running experiments and trial-and-error much more difficult. Furthermore, reinforcement learning methods are generally complex and require very careful tuning to achieve good results. For example, they are sensitive to hyperparameter settings and training data. As result, reinforcement learning methods are relatively fragile. When training on massive scale, ensuring that the system runs stably (for instance, making sure the training loss decreases steadily) is not just machine learning problem, but also an engineering challenge.

sections.title: 6.4.4.2 More Synthetic Data for Reasoning
sections.content: Because high-quality human annotations for complex multi-step reasoning are scarce, scaling training data often relies on synthetic data generation. Instead of manually writing step-by-step proofs, researchers use strong LLMs to generate diverse reasoning trajectories, which are then filtered and curated to train new models [Zelikman et al., 2022; Mukherjee et al., 2023]. To generate synthetic data for reasoning, common approach is to sample multiple reasoning paths from teacher models for given seed question [Wang et al., 2023b]. We can then apply verifiers or execution environments to evaluate these paths, and retain only those that arrive at the correct final answer through sound logical steps. Furthermore, models can be used to generate variations of existing problems (e.g., changing numerical values or structural constraints in math and coding tasks) to expand the distribution of training data.

sections.title: 6.4.4.3 Scaling Context Length
sections.content: As reasoning models tackle increasingly complex problems, the length of reasoning paths has become primary bottleneck. The demand for large context windows in reasoning arises from several sources. First, to elicit deep System 2 thinking, the input prompt itself often requires extensive context. This includes detailed logical constraints, complex environment rules, or multiple long few-shot CoT examples. Second, the generated reasoning process for complex task can easily span thousands or even tens of thousands of tokens before arriving at the final conclusion. Third, recent advances in LLM agents have also increased the demand for reasoning. Agentic reasoning often extends over many rounds of interaction, creating an even greater need for long 6.5 Evaluating Reasoning LLMs 271 context windows. This demand has directly driven the LLM industry to develop models that support massive context windows. For instance, many LLMs now support context lengths of up to 128K tokens, and more advanced models, such as Anthropics Claude 3.5 [Anthropic, 2024] and Googles Gemini 1.5 [Google, 2024], support hundreds of thousands of tokens, or even one million tokens. The interested reader may refer to Chapter 2 for more detailed discussion on long-context LLMs. However, handling long contexts for reasoning leads to new challenges that go beyond general context compression. In tasks like summarizing long novel or extracting key points from documents, an LLM can afford to compress information and lose minor details. In contrast, reasoning requires strict, high-precision logical continuity. Every intermediate step is critical link in heavily interdependent chain. If the model forgets specific assumption defined in the prompt, or loses track of variable calculated in step 2 while executing step 50, the entire derivation collapses. Therefore, scaling context for reasoning is not just about expanding the KV cache to store more tokens. It requires the model to achieve reliable retrieval across long distances and to maintain strict logical consistency.

sections.title: 6.5 Evaluating Reasoning LLMs
sections.content: In this section, we discuss how to evaluate reasoning LLMs. This task is similar to evaluating standard LLMs [Chang et al., 2024b]. However, reasoning problems are so complex that we often need more detailed evaluation and other special considerations.

sections.title: 6.5.1 Outcome-based vs. Process-based Evaluation
sections.content: When evaluating how well an LLM reasons, the easiest and most common method is outcomebased evaluation. In this approach, we only look at the final answer produced by the model. If the final answer matches the ground truth, the model is considered correct. This method is widely used in popular reasoning benchmarks, such as GSM8K [Cobbe et al., 2021] and MATH [Hendrycks et al., 2021b]. However, outcome-based evaluation has the right answer for the wrong reason problem, also known as false positive. model might generate flawed logical steps but accidentally arrive at the correct final number. If we only check the final outcome, we might incorrectly conclude that the model possesses strong reasoning capabilities when it just got lucky. For more detailed evaluation, we can use process-based evaluation. Instead of just checking the final answer, we can examine the entire reasoning path step by step [Wang et al., 2024c; Xia et al., 2025]. model is only considered correct if both its intermediate logic and its final conclusion are sound. This is an ideal method but is very difficult to implement in practice. The main challenge is that step-level gold data is scarce and expensive to create. Furthermore, for any complex problem, there is an exponentially large number of valid reasoning paths. It is infeasible to manually list all correct intermediate steps for every path model might take. To make process-based evaluation more practical, we can narrow the scope to evaluate local reasoning decisions. One approach is to reduce the problem to simple next-step evaluation task: given correct sequence of previous steps, we check whether the reasoning model can correctly choose or generate the next logical step. To do this, it is straightforward to use PRMs to evaluate 272 Reasoning the quality of each step generated by the LLM. This method is also related to reward model evaluation [Lambert et al., 2025]. Instead of examining the output of the reasoning model, we assess the quality of the PRMs. Furthermore, we can consider the fundamental capabilities of reasoning models, such as their ability to identify errors in given reasoning path. This can also be viewed as test of their meta-reasoning abilities: we ask the model not just to reason, but to evaluate the reasoning process itself [Zeng et al., 2024]. In practice, process-based evaluation is not based on single standard. We can judge the quality of reasoning step from different angles, such as logical consistency, coherence, and objectivity [Lee and Hockenmaier, 2025]. However, while process-based evaluation is much more detailed, it comes with much higher annotation cost, and is often not robust enough. Therefore, most real-world research still relies on the simpler outcome-based evaluation.

Alternatively, LLMs can be used to compare two reasoning models. The judge is presented with the outputs from both models for the same query and decides which reasoning path is superior, or if the result is tie. The win rate then reflects the percentage of times specific model is preferred.

sections.title: 6.5.3 Open Issues
sections.content: One issue is data contamination. As language models are trained on increasingly massive datasets collected from the internet, it becomes very difficult to keep test data out of the training process. If model has already seen the questions from reasoning benchmark (like MATH or GSM8K) during its pre-training phase, it might simply be reciting memorized solution instead of actually reasoning on the fly. This makes it hard to determine whether high benchmark scores reflect true problem-solving abilities or just good memory. To address this, the community is encouraged to explore new benchmarks, where problems are updated continuously, as well as private hold-out sets that are never released to the public. Another issue is robustness. Current reasoning models are sometimes fragile. model might solve complex math problem perfectly, but fail completely if the exact same question is rephrased slightly or if irrelevant details are added to the prompt. This sensitivity suggests that models sometimes rely on superficial text patterns rather than truly understanding the underlying logic. For more robust reasoning, we need LLMs to easily adapt to new or even more challenging tasks. Moreover, LLMs may generate hallucinated or unfaithful reasoning paths. For example, they might invent fake mathematical rules to reach conclusion. In some cases, the generated text might look like perfect logical deduction, but the model actually arrived at the answer via hidden mechanism (such as lucky guess or memorized shortcut). This unfaithfulness highlights 274 Reasoning gap between the text the model outputs and its actual internal representations. In reinforcement learning setups, this is often related to the reward hacking problem. If models are only rewarded for the final answer, they often learn to cheat the reward system with flawed logic. Therefore, it is valuable to introduce step-by-step supervision in RL, such as process supervision, to check if each intermediate step is truly correct. The fourth issue is benchmark saturation. The rapid progress of reasoning LLMs means that standard evaluation benchmarks are quickly becoming outdated. Models are now achieving nearperfect scores on tests that were considered extremely difficult just year or two ago. This benchmark saturation makes it difficult to compare new models or measure real progress in the field. Therefore, researchers need to develop harder tests that evaluate true logical derivation on novel problems. Note that human-level reasoning is often open-ended and interactive. An alternative approach to testing reasoning models might be to use them in autonomous agents, which can explore, use external tools, and recover from their own errors.

sections.title: 6.6 Remarks
sections.content: We now discuss some interesting issues related to reasoning LLMs.

sections.title: 6.6.1 External Reasoning vs. Internal Reasoning
sections.content: In previous discussions, we assumed that the reasoning process can be well captured by textbased reasoning path (e.g., CoT). This raises fundamental question: Does the generated CoT text actually reflect how the model reasons? This inquiry leads us to examine the distinction between externalized reasoning and the true internal thinking processes. When we prompt an LLM to think step by step, we are forcing it to externalize its computation into discrete tokens. However, we cannot simply view this text sequence as the actual reasoning process. On one hand, an LLM might generate detailed and logically sound CoT, but the actual decision-making might have already occurred implicitly within the hidden representations of the very first few tokens. On the other hand, model might produce flawed or nonsensical CoT, yet still output the correct final answer, suggesting that its internal representations are tracking the task differently from what the generated text implies. Researchers have demonstrated that CoT explanations can be deceptive [Turpin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025]. For example, LLMs may have bias towards generating logical CoT to reach an incorrect answer, though the correct answer has been mentioned in the prompt. To uncover how LLMs actually think, researchers are turning to neuron activation analysis and mechanistic interpretability. The goal is to understand what happens inside the hidden layers of an LLM during the generation process. For example, in Fraser-Taliente et al. [2026]s work, natural language auto-encoders are used to convert the activations into natural language text. natural language auto-encoder consists of an activation verbalizer and an activation reconstructor, which are used to directly map internal residual stream activations into human-readable text and back. In this way, we can decode these activations to read the thoughts of LLMs. Another line of research focuses on reasoning without text, called latent reasoning or implicit reasoning. In standard reasoning, as we defined earlier, reasoning path consists of sequence of text steps. In latent reasoning, this process happens internally before the model speaks. This 6.6 Remarks is achieved either by replacing discrete tokens with continuous vectors or by generating actual text words in the background that are kept hidden from the user. Here we present some of these methods. One of the simplest ideas is the use of pause tokens. As is standard in autoregressive generation, language model gets one step of internal calculation for every word it outputs. Interestingly, it is discovered that if we feed the model dummy tokens (called pause tokens), the model gets extra computational time to process information in its hidden layers before it has to output the final answer [Goyal et al., 2024]. This shows that LLMs could perform silent computations or latent thinking without generating real words. Another approach uses knowledge distillation to compress explicit reasoning into hidden states. For instance, the implicit chain of thought method trains student model to directly mimic the hidden internal states of larger teacher model that is thinking out loud [Deng et al., 2023]. As result, the student model learns to skip generating the text. Alternatively, the LLM can also learn from itself using self-distillation techniques [Shen et al., 2025]. We can force the latent thinking process to match the final hidden states of the text-based reasoning. In both methods, latent thinking is embodied as continuous mathematical space: instead of generating step-by-step sequence of readable text, the model computes the reasoning steps using hidden vector-based representations. An alternative method to reason in continuous latent spaces is to use the chain of continuous thought (COCONUT) paradigm [Hao et al., 2025]. In standard text generation, the output of the final layer is converted into discrete token, which is then fed back into the first layer for the next step. This process forces the model to compress its internal computation into single token. COCONUT bypasses this step during the reasoning phase. It takes the output vector from the last layer and feeds it directly back into the input layer as continuous thought. By repeating this process, the model builds chain of continuous vectors before it starts generating the final text answer. Because continuous vectors can hold more information than discrete tokens, the model can explore multiple reasoning paths at the same time without committing to specific token choice early on. This approach demonstrates that LLMs do not have to rely on human language to solve complex problems. By keeping the reasoning process in continuous space, they can compute answers more efficiently. Instead of performing reasoning in continuous space, we can also use normal text tokens to represent internal thoughts. For example, in the Quiet-STaR method [Zelikman et al., 2024], the model is trained to think quietly, right in the middle of reading or writing normal text. The idea is simple: before the model predicts the next token, it generates short sequence of hidden thought tokens. You can think of this as an inner monologue or quick mental scratchpad that the user never sees. After generating these hidden thoughts, the LLM uses them to help guess the actual next word. If these thoughts help the LLM predict the correct word, the LLM is rewarded and learns that this way of thinking is useful. If the thoughts are useless or confusing, the LLM learns to discard them. Reasoning

sections.title: 6.6.2 Memorization vs. Reasoning
sections.content: When discussing LLMs, question often arises: Is the model truly thinking, or does it simply have big memory and is reciting similar answer it saw in its training data? This leads to the discussion on comparing reasoning and memorization in LLMs. Simply put, the difference between the two can be summarized as follows: Memorization is looking backward. The model adjusts its parameters to learn patterns from the training data. When faced with similar input, the model simply replays the learned patterns. Reasoning is moving forward. Instead of searching for ready-made answer, the model applies general rules and logic to build chain of thought step by step. The core of reasoning is generalization, even when facing completely new problem that never appeared in the training set, the model can solve it using logical tools. In early deep learning research, this boundary was not always clear. For example, Zhang et al. [2021] point out that deep neural networks have massive memorization capacity, easily memorizing noisy data with completely random labels. For LLMs, given their huge model sizes, they can not only memorize Wikipedia but also details hidden inside code repositories. This memorization ability often disguises itself as reasoning. For example, if we prompt an LLM with classic algorithm problem but tweak the numbers slightly, the LLM might rely on its memory inertia and output the original answer anyway, thus making basic mistake. This is often referred to as the stochastic parrots phenomenon [Bender et al., 2021], which means that the LLM is blindly mimicking and stitching together memorized text without truly understanding the underlying logic. To better see the difference between memorization and reasoning, we can look at two different dimensions.

sections.title: 6.6.2.1 Grokking and Generalization
sections.content: When exploring how models transition from memorization to true understanding, researchers has made an interesting discovery called grokking [Power et al., 2022]. They train small Transformer model to learn binary operations in abstract algebra (such as modular addition). They notice very interesting phenomenon: early in training, the model quickly reached 100% accuracy on the training set, but its accuracy on the test set was almost zero. At this stage, the model is clearly just memorizing equations by rote. However, if they do not stop training and let the model continue looping over the data long past the point of overfitting, something surprising happens. Suddenly, the test accuracy spikes to 100% in very short time. The model seems to experience an aha moment. Further studies show that before this aha moment, the model parameters are messily memorizing specific equations (like 2 + 3 = 5) [Nanda et al., 2023]. But when grokking occurs, the 6.6 Remarks 277 network internally develops general mathematical representation using trigonometric functions and Fourier transforms. It has found universal algorithm that can explain all the data. This experiment tells us that reasoning does not appear out of nowhere. It often emerges as high-level generalization state when memorization hits bottleneck, or after extensive training, where the network organizes its parameters to find the most universal explanation. 6.6.2.2 The Cost Trade-off From the perspective of information theory and computational efficiency, LLMs naturally balance memorization and reasoning based on cost. On one hand, memorization requires more parameter capacity. To memorize every fact in the world, the model size would need to grow infinitely. On the other hand, reasoning requires more computational steps at inference time. As long as model memorizes the general rules of addition and multiplication, it can solve many math problems by taking such computational steps during generation. Therefore, LLMs usually take the path of least resistance. For common facts, retrieving the answer directly from parameters (or memory) is the fastest way. But for rare, multi-step tasks, using System 2 thinking is more suitable way. This also explains why techniques like RAG have become popular. The essence of RAG is to offload the burden of memory to an external database, and thus we can free up the parameter space for reasoning. By separating knowledge retrieval from logical deduction, the LLM no longer needs to memorize ever-changing external facts. Instead, it knows how to look things up and process them.

sections.title: 6.6.3 Can LLMs Truly Reason?
sections.content: The question of whether LLMs can truly reason is one of the most debated topics in AI today. When we see an LLM perfectly solve math problem or write complex schedule, it is very tempting to believe that it understands the world just as human does. However, to answer this question, we must look at how these models actually work. Essentially, LLMs work by predicting the next word. Because these models have processed massive amounts of text, they have completely mastered the rules, grammar, and structure of human language. In cognitive science, this is known as formal linguistic competence [Chomsky, 1965; Mahowald et al., 2024]. They know exactly how words should be logically ordered. However, they struggle with functional linguistic competence, which is the ability to use language to understand and navigate the real world [Kambhampati et al., 2024]. Unlike humans, who learn by physically interacting with their environment, LLMs only know the underlying patterns of text. Because they are not grounded in the real world, they lack true understanding of physical space and strict cause-and-effect [Mahowald et al., 2024]. This limitation becomes obvious when we test LLMs on planning tasks [Valmeekam et al., 2023]. For example, for classical planning problems, such as moving colored blocks on table into specific stack, the LLM can often solve the problem if it uses common words they had seen in their training data. But if the names of the blocks and the actions are replaced with nonsense words, the performance dropped drastically [Kambhampati, 2024]. true reasoning system would not care about the names, because the underlying mathematical logic is exactly the 278 Reasoning same. The LLM fails because its familiar text pattern is broken. Furthermore, techniques like CoT prompting force the model to output step-by-step process. This shows some behavior of slow and deliberate human thought. But in reality, the LLM is still just moving strictly forward, and predicts what logical explanation usually looks like. If the LLM makes mistake or holds biased assumption, it will often confidently generate flawed explanation simply to justify its wrong answer [Chen et al., 2025]. Ultimately, to answer whether LLMs can truly reason, we first need to define what true reasoning actually means. If we expect LLMs to think exactly like humans, it is clear from the discussion above that there are some differences. However, if we view reasoning purely as functional process, the answer changes. Reasoning can be defined simply as the ability to take complex problem, break it down, apply logical rules, and arrive at correct conclusion. When an LLM correctly solves math equation step by step, or when it writes logical piece of code to process data, it is executing valid logical chain. Even if this ability emerges from training largescale neural networks rather than human-like cognition, the outcome is still successful problemsolving. As LLMs grow larger and learn from more data, they move beyond simply memorizing answers and start capturing the underlying rules of logic.

sections.title: 6.7 Summary
sections.content: In this chapter, we have presented how to apply LLMs to reasoning, which is considered one of the most challenging tasks in NLP. In particular, we have discussed methods of improving reasoning abilities in the training and inference phases. We have also studied evaluation methods for reasoning LLMs, as well as some open problems. The finding that LLMs can explicitly map out their reasoning steps has inspired new research directions and practical applications. Instead of viewing reasoning only as way to answer isolated questions, current research treats reasoning as tool that drives more complex and autonomous behaviors. First, reasoning has been closely related to the concept of long thinking, which fundamentally changes how computational power is used in LLMs. As we discussed earlier in Section 6.3, by giving models more time and computational power to think, they can solve much harder problems. This brings big change to how LLMs work: we now need to figure out how to best distribute computing power while the model is generating an answer, rather than just during its initial training. Solving this at the system level is beyond the scope of this book. However, building highly efficient reasoning models that know how much time to spend thinking is very promising and practical research direction. Second, the ability to reason has been the basis of agentic reasoning, where LLMs stop being passive answering machines and become active participants in an environment. In standard text generation, reasoning is straight line from prompt to answer. Agentic reasoning, by contrast, operates in continuous loop of thinking, acting, and observing [Yao et al., 2023]. However, this loop leads to big challenges. The issue is that LLMs can easily get lost or stuck in the loop. They might repeat the same mistakes, make bad plans, or not know how to recover from failures when an action fails [Shinn et al., 2023]. Keeping the model on track over long time is still very hard. Third, reasoning directly enables tool-augmented reasoning, which solves the limitations of LLMs, such as their inability to perform precise math or access real-time facts. Instead of forcing 6.7 Summary 279 the LLM to guess an answer, we can train the LLM to recognize its own limits and write code [Gao et al., 2023b] or call external APIs [Schick et al., 2024] to do the heavy lifting. However, the main problem is teaching the LLM when it needs tool and which one to pick out of many [Qin et al., 2024]. Also, if tool breaks or returns weird data, the LLM must be smart enough to catch the error and try again, rather than just trusting the bad result.
